The central finding: the post describes § 56-5-3890 in its pre-2025 form ('wireless electronic communications devices', 'primarily focuses on texting') — the section was rewritten by 2025 Act No. 40 into a hands-free law effective 2025-09-01 that expressly permits 'an earpiece or device worn on a wrist to conduct voice-based communication' and listening to audio content on a device that is not held, and that penalizes a first offense with a flat $100 fine and assesses two points only on a second or subsequent offense within three years. verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina does not have a specific law that directly prohibits wearing headphones or AirPods while driving in Charleston. However, this does not mean the practice is completely legal or without consequences.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code Title 56 Chapter 5 (Uniform Act Regulating Traffic on Highways), read in full for 'headphone', 'earphone', 'earbud', 'headset', 'earpiece' — the only hit is § 56-5-3890(B)(1), which permits an earpiece; City of Charleston Code Ch. 19 has no headphone section
verifiedClaims.note: Correct. No state statute or Charleston ordinance bans headphones or earbuds. The second sentence is supported by Charleston City Code § 19-178 (careless operation) and by comparative fault.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina operates under broader distracted driving laws that could apply to headphone use. The law (SC Code Section 56-5-3890) prohibits drivers from using wireless electronic communications devices while driving a vehicle. Although this law primarily focuses on drivers texting, it also applies to any activity that can impair a driver’s ability to drive safely.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: South Carolina's distracted driving statute, S.C. Code § 56-5-3890, was rewritten by the South Carolina Hands-Free and Distracted Driving Act (2025 Act No. 40) effective September 1, 2025. It now prohibits a driver from holding or supporting a mobile electronic device with any part of the body, from reading, composing or transmitting text, and from watching video on the device. It expressly allows 'an earpiece or device worn on a wrist to conduct voice-based communication' and listening to audio-based content or using navigation so long as the device is not held. The statute says nothing about headphones or earbuds as such, and it does not reach 'any activity that can impair' driving — it lists specific prohibited acts.
verifiedClaims.note: Most consequential finding. The post's description ('wireless electronic communications devices', 'primarily focuses on drivers texting') is the 2014 version of the section. Verbatim today: '(B) While operating a motor vehicle on any public highway of this State, a person shall not: (1) hold or support, with any part of the body, a mobile electronic device. This provision does not prohibit the use of an earpiece or device worn on a wrist to conduct voice-based communication; (2) read, compose, or transmit any text ...; (3) watch motion including ... a video, movie, game, or video call'. (C)(6)(a) exempts 'navigation, listening to audio-based content, or obtaining traffic and road condition information in a manner that does not require the operator to type, provided that the device is not held'. The last sentence of the claim ('any activity that can impair') has no basis in the statute and must go. Use the strict citation form 'S.C. Code § 56-5-3890', not 'SC Code Section 56-5-3890'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Charleston police officers can cite drivers for "careless operation" if they determine headphone use is preventing safe vehicle operation. This falls under South Carolina's broader statutes regarding negligent or reckless driving.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Within the city limits, Charleston police can cite a driver under City of Charleston Code § 19-178, 'Careless operation of a vehicle', which makes it unlawful 'to operate any vehicle without care and caution and full regard for the safety of persons and property'. That is a city ordinance, not a state statute. South Carolina's state-level offense is reckless driving, S.C. Code § 56-5-2920, which requires 'a wilful or wanton disregard for the safety of persons or property' — a higher bar than carelessness.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: City of Charleston Code of Ordinances § 19-178 (Code 1975, § 33-32), Municode, online content updated 2026-09-03; S.C. Code § 56-5-2920
verifiedClaims.note: 'Careless operation' is real but it is the city ordinance § 19-178, not a state statute; the word 'careless' does not appear anywhere in S.C. Code Title 56 Chapter 5. The second sentence mis-attributes it to 'South Carolina's broader statutes'. Reckless driving § 56-5-2920 verbatim: 'Any person who drives any vehicle in such a manner as to indicate either a wilful or wanton disregard for the safety of persons or property is guilty of reckless driving' (fine $25-$200 or up to 30 days; 6 points under § 56-1-720).

verifiedClaims.claim: While South Carolina does not explicitly ban truck drivers from using headphones, they are subject to stricter regulations regarding their use. Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration rules, company policies, and heightened professional standards restrict the use of headphones for truckers and delivery drivers.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration rules do not mention headphones; they prohibit texting while driving a commercial motor vehicle (49 CFR 392.80) and using a hand-held mobile telephone while driving a CMV (49 CFR 392.82), and they bar motor carriers from allowing or requiring either. Hands-free use, including an earpiece, is not prohibited by those sections. Company policies commonly go further.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: 49 CFR 392.80 (Prohibition against texting); 49 CFR 392.82 (Using a hand-held mobile telephone)
verifiedClaims.note: Verbatim § 392.82(a)(1): 'No driver shall use a hand-held mobile telephone while driving a CMV.' (a)(2): 'No motor carrier shall allow or require its drivers to use a hand-held mobile telephone while driving a CMV.' Neither section restricts headphones. 'Heightened professional standards' is rhetoric; harmless if kept. The internal link target was not re-checked today.

verifiedClaims.claim: DOT inspectors, who are common in Charleston’s port areas, may flag headphone use as a safety concern.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: No FMCSA or SC State Transport Police source located that treats headphone use as an inspection item
verifiedClaims.note: Roadside inspections (49 CFR Part 396 / CVSA criteria) examine the vehicle and driver credentials, hours of service and impairment; headphone use is not an inspection item in any primary source found. Unverifiable — drop the sentence.

verifiedClaims.claim: Some commercial drivers may use single-ear Bluetooth devices exclusively for work-related communication, but not for entertainment. This "one-ear exception" requires maintaining awareness of surrounding traffic sounds.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Federal rules allow a commercial driver to use a hands-free earpiece for calls (49 CFR 392.82 bars only hand-held phone use), and South Carolina's § 56-5-3890(B)(1) likewise permits 'an earpiece ... to conduct voice-based communication'. Neither rule uses the phrase 'one-ear exception' or limits the earpiece to work calls.
verifiedClaims.note: 'One-ear exception' is not a term in the FMCSRs or the S.C. Code. Reword as a description of what hands-free rules allow rather than a named exception; drop the quotation marks and the 'exclusively for work-related communication' limit, which no rule imposes.

verifiedClaims.claim: Commercial insurance policies may deny claims involving driver distraction, and companies could face liability.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: A trucking company can be liable for its driver's negligence, and commercial policies vary in what they cover.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: General law of employer liability; no primary source supports a general 'may deny claims involving driver distraction' statement
verifiedClaims.note: The employer-liability half is standard (respondeat superior); the insurance-denial half is unverifiable as a general statement and should be softened or removed.

verifiedClaims.claim: Additionally, drivers might face CDL suspension if cited for distracted driving while using headphones.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: A commercial driver convicted of texting or of using a hand-held mobile telephone while driving a CMV commits a 'serious traffic violation'; a second such conviction within three years brings a CDL disqualification of at least 60 days and a third at least 120 days (49 CFR 383.51, Table 2). Headphone use by itself is not a listed violation.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: 49 CFR 383.51(c), Table 2, items (9) and (10)
verifiedClaims.note: Table 2 to § 383.51: '(9) Violating a State or local law or ordinance on motor vehicle traffic control prohibiting texting while driving a CMV — 60 days [second conviction within 3 years] / 120 days [third]'; '(10) ... restricting or prohibiting the use of a hand-held mobile telephone while driving a CMV — 60 days / 120 days'. The disqualification attaches to a conviction under a state hands-free/texting law such as § 56-5-3890, not to wearing headphones. 'Suspension' should read 'disqualification'.

The section may say so in one sentence but must not claim the statute bans headphones.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina does not have laws that prevent drivers from wearing headphones. However, that does not mean that there are no legal consequences. Drivers may face repercussions if wearing headphones causes them to miss a stop sign, run a red light, or commit any other traffic violations.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code Title 56 Chapter 5 (no headphone provision); § 56-1-720 (disobedience of any official traffic control device: 4 points)
verifiedClaims.note: Correct. The underlying violation (stop sign, red light) carries its own penalty and 4 points under § 56-1-720.

verifiedClaims.claim: A fine of up to $100 for a first offense
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Under the hands-free law, a first distracted-driving offense is a flat $100 fine, 'no part of which may be suspended'; a second or subsequent offense within three years is $200 plus two points. A separate moving violation caused by inattention — running a red light or stop sign — carries its own fine (up to $100 under the chapter's general penalty, § 56-5-6190, unless another penalty applies) and four points.
verifiedClaims.note: The post's only dollar figure. As a hands-free penalty it is wrong ('up to' — the statute fixes it at $100, none suspendable); as a general-penalty figure it happens to match § 56-5-6190 ('not more than one hundred dollars or by imprisonment for not more than thirty days'). Verbatim § 56-5-3890(D)(1): '(a) for a first offense, must be fined one hundred dollars, no part of which may be suspended; (b) for a second or subsequent offense, must be fined two hundred dollars, no part of which may be suspended, and must have two points assessed'. (D)(2): only offenses within three years count as priors. The penalties list should say which offense it is describing.

verifiedClaims.claim: Two points added to your driving record
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Two points are assessed only for a second or subsequent distracted-driving offense within three years under § 56-5-3890(D)(1)(b); a first offense carries no points. Running a red light or stop sign is four points (disobedience of any official traffic control device).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 56-5-3890(D)(1)(b); § 56-1-720 schedule ('Distracted driving (second or subsequent offense) — 2'; 'Disobedience of any official traffic control device — 4')
verifiedClaims.note: The § 56-1-720 schedule was amended by 2025 Act No. 40 § 3 (eff. 2025-09-01) to add 'Distracted driving (second or subsequent offense) 2'. The post's flat 'two points' is wrong for a first offense and wrong for the red-light/stop-sign example it gives.

verifiedClaims.claim: Increased insurance premiums resulting from the citation
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Hedged consequence ('may face'); no figure asserted

verifiedClaims.claim: In cases where you and the other party contributed to the crash, you may be found partially responsible. Under comparative negligence rules, the claim amounts would then be reduced based on your level of fault.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243, 399 S.E.2d 783 (S.C. 1991)
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from facts-2586/facts-4729. Nelson: a plaintiff 'may recover damages if his or her negligence is not greater than that of the defendant. The amount of the plaintiff's recovery shall be reduced in proportion to the amount of his or her negligence.' Optional: add the 51% bar and attribute to Nelson; never cite § 15-38-15 (profile rule).

verifiedClaims.claim: While it is not illegal to wear headphones or AirPods in South Carolina, if it is determined that wearing them contributed to a crash in some way, it could make you more liable for any resulting damages.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code Title 56 Chapter 5 (no headphone ban); Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co. (comparative fault); § 56-5-6160
verifiedClaims.note: Correct. Because no statute is violated by wearing headphones, negligence per se is not available on that fact alone; headphone use is ordinary-negligence evidence weighed under comparative fault. If the driver was also holding a phone, texting or watching video, a § 56-5-3890 violation can support negligence per se — but under § 56-5-6160 ('No evidence of conviction of any person for any violation of this chapter shall be admissible in any court in any civil action') the ticket or conviction itself does not come in; the conduct must be proven with witnesses and other evidence. Cosmetic: this heading is the only one wrapped in <strong> and lacks an id/TOC entry; the body also carries a stray data-teams span.

verifiedClaims.claim: Many newer vehicles automatically adjust the volume based on speed, allowing you to hear important sounds, such as sirens and horns.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Consumer-product description (speed-sensitive volume), non-legal, non-statistical
verifiedClaims.note: Hedged ('many'); no figure. Acceptable.

verifiedClaims.claim: Take photos/video that clearly show the other driver wearing headphones
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Practical advice; consistent with proving the conduct by evidence other than a citation (§ 56-5-6160)
verifiedClaims.note: Advice, not a factual claim. Keep the 'do not accuse' line.

verifiedClaims.claim: Inform an officer about the headphone use in the official police report. A police report is key evidence and could include the officer's observation if they notice the other driver wearing headphones.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: SCDPS TR-310 Traffic Collision Report Manual (contributing-factor codes 02 Distracted/Inattention, 19 Cell Phone, 20 Texting); S.C. Code § 56-5-1290
verifiedClaims.note: The officer records a primary contributing factor on the TR-310; 'Distracted/Inattention' is code 02, so headphone use can be reflected as distraction if the officer is told or observes it. Caution for the refresher: § 56-5-1290 provides that the collision report itself 'may [not] be evidence of the negligence or due care of either party at the trial', though officers may use it to refresh recollection — so 'key evidence' is true for the claim stage, not as a trial exhibit. Do not overstate.

verifiedClaims.claim: When you leave the car accident scene, seek medical attention even if you believe that you have minor injuries. You should also protect your legal rights by consulting with a licensed and trusted attorney.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Standard advice; S.C. Code § 15-3-530(5) (three-year limitation) if a deadline is added
verifiedClaims.note: No deadline is stated in the post. If one is added it is three years from the crash, S.C. Code § 15-3-530 (verified in facts-1740 on 2026-09-24).

verifiedClaims.claim: Although South Carolina does not ban headphone usage while driving, wearing wireless headsets or earbuds can become a distraction for drivers.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code Title 56 Chapter 5; § 56-5-3890(B)(1) (earpiece permitted)

verifiedClaims.claim: The rules around headphone and earbud use while driving are worth confirming before you rely on them, and enforcement differs from the position for hands-free systems built into a vehicle.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: No. South Carolina has no statute that bans headphones or earbuds while driving. The state's hands-free law, S.C. Code § 56-5-3890 (effective September 1, 2025), prohibits holding a phone, texting and watching video, but expressly allows an earpiece for voice calls and listening to audio on a device you are not holding. Inside Charleston, police can still cite careless operation under City Code § 19-178 if headphone use leads to unsafe driving, and headphone use can count against you in a comparative-fault claim.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 56-5-3890(B)(1), (C)(6)(a); City of Charleston Code § 19-178
verifiedClaims.note: The current answer does not answer the question and renders into FAQPage structured data. Replace with a direct answer.

verifiedClaims.claim: A vehicle's Bluetooth system plays through the car's speakers, leaving both ears open to traffic sounds. Headphones and AirPods block or mask those sounds, which is the safety distinction that matters.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Descriptive; legally, § 56-5-3890(C)(7) exempts manufacturer-installed equipment and (B)(1) permits an earpiece
verifiedClaims.note: Accurate as a safety distinction. Optional one clause: 'and the hands-free law treats manufacturer-installed systems as exempt'.

verifiedClaims.claim: They compromise auditory awareness, cutting you off from sirens, horns and the sounds of an approaching hazard, and they increase cognitive load by adding another stream of information to process.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Safety reasoning; no figure asserted
verifiedClaims.note: Keep. Do not add a headphone-specific statistic; none exists in NHTSA or SCDPS data.

verifiedClaims.claim: Commercial drivers are subject to their own federal regulations in addition to state rules, so a practice that goes unremarked for a private driver can put a commercial licence at real risk.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Commercial drivers are subject to federal rules in addition to state law: 49 CFR 392.80 bans texting and 49 CFR 392.82 bans hand-held phone use while driving a commercial motor vehicle, and a second conviction within three years brings a CDL disqualification of at least 60 days (49 CFR 383.51). Those rules do not name headphones, but many carriers prohibit them by policy.
verifiedClaims.note: The answer is directionally right but says nothing concrete, and 'licence' is British spelling — use 'license'. The CDL consequence attaches to texting/hand-held convictions, not to headphones as such.

verifiedClaims.claim: It supports the argument that they were not driving attentively. Witness observations and any admission at the scene are worth recording, since headphone use is not visible in a police report by default.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: It supports the argument that they were not driving attentively, and because no statute bans headphones the claim is proven as ordinary negligence under South Carolina's comparative-fault rule. Photos, witness observations and any admission at the scene matter: the officer's TR-310 collision report can record 'distracted/inattention' as a contributing factor, but only if the officer observes it or is told, and the report itself is not admissible to prove negligence at trial.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: SCDPS TR-310 Report Manual (code 02 Distracted/Inattention); S.C. Code § 56-5-1290; Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.
verifiedClaims.note: 'Not visible in a police report by default' is roughly right — there is no headphone code — but the report has a distraction code, so the fix is to tell the officer. Minor reword.

recommendedEdits: Rewrite the 'What South Carolina Law Says' paragraph on § 56-5-3890: it is now the South Carolina Hands-Free and Distracted Driving Act (2025 Act No. 40, effective September 1, 2025) — prohibits holding or supporting a mobile electronic device, texting, and watching video; expressly allows an earpiece for voice calls, listening to audio and navigation on a device that is not held, and manufacturer-installed systems; drop 'wireless electronic communications devices', 'primarily focuses on drivers texting' and 'applies to any activity that can impair'.
Cite it as 'S.C. Code § 56-5-3890' (strict profile format), not 'SC Code Section 56-5-3890', and link https://www.scstatehouse.gov/code/t56c005.php.

Correct the 'careless operation' sentence: it is City of Charleston Code § 19-178 ('Careless operation of a vehicle'), a city ordinance, not a South Carolina statute; the state offense is reckless driving, S.C. Code § 56-5-2920, which requires wilful or wanton disregard.

Fix the penalties list: first distracted-driving offense is a flat $100 fine (none suspendable), second or subsequent within three years $200 plus two points (§ 56-5-3890(D)); a first offense carries no points; the 180-day warnings-only period that began 2025-09-01 has ended. If the list is meant to describe a red-light or stop-sign violation instead, that is four points under § 56-1-720 — say which offense the list describes.
Change 'A fine of up to $100 for a first offense' to 'A $100 fine for a first distracted-driving offense ($200 for a second or later offense within three years)'.
Change 'Two points added to your driving record' to 'Two points on a second or subsequent distracted-driving offense (none on a first)'.

statuteCitations.name: Unlawful use of a mobile electronic device while operating a motor vehicle — South Carolina Hands-Free and Distracted Driving Act (2025 Act No. 40, H.3276), effective 2025-09-01; permits an earpiece for voice communication and unheld audio/navigation; $100 first offense, $200 plus two points for a second or subsequent offense within three years; preempts local ordinances on mobile-device use
South Carolina Hands-Free and Distracted Driving Act — § 5: warnings only for the first 180 days after 2025-09-01; § 8: takes effect September 1, 2025

Point system schedule — 'Distracted driving (second or subsequent offense)' 2 points; 'Disobedience of any official traffic control device' 4 points; reckless driving 6 points (amended by 2025 Act No. 40 § 3)
Reckless driving — wilful or wanton disregard for the safety of persons or property; $25-$200 or up to 30 days
Evidence of conviction inadmissible in civil action — 'No evidence of conviction of any person for any violation of this chapter shall be admissible in any court in any civil action'
General penalty for violations of chapter — fine of not more than $100 or imprisonment not more than 30 days where no other penalty is provided
Evidentiary use of collision reports — reports may not be evidence of negligence or due care at trial; officers may use them to refresh recollection
Three-year limitation for injury to the person (subsection (5)) — only if a filing deadline is added

Careless operation of a vehicle — 'unlawful for any person to operate any vehicle without care and caution and full regard for the safety of persons and property' (Code 1975, § 33-32); Municode content updated 2026-09-03

Unlawful use of a handheld electronic communication device (Ord. 2013-107) — $100, no points; note S.C. Code § 56-5-3890(G) preempts local ordinances on mobile-device use, so cite the state statute, not this ordinance, for phone use
Using a hand-held mobile telephone — no CMV driver may use a hand-held mobile telephone while driving; carriers may not allow or require it
Prohibition against texting while driving a CMV
CDL disqualification — Table 2 serious traffic violations include texting and hand-held phone use while driving a CMV; second conviction within 3 years 60 days, third 120 days
